rules.statement: In a test project, unit tests must be hermetic: they don't touch the network, real clock, file system or other external state, and fake every dependency instead.
rules.why: The family's testing conventions require unit tests to be hermetic so they are deterministic and run anywhere.
rules.check: Look for unit tests that make real HTTP calls, read real files or environment state, use the system clock, or depend on external services instead of fakes.

rules.statement: In a test project, create mocks with `MockBehavior.Strict`, not the default loose behavior.
rules.why: The family's testing conventions require strict mocks so an unexpected call fails the test instead of silently returning a default.

rules.statement: In a test project, name unit test methods `Method_State_Expected`.
rules.why: The family's testing conventions name each test for the member under test, the state it runs in and the expected outcome.
rules.check: Look for test methods whose names don't follow the three-part `Method_State_Expected` pattern.

rules.statement: Keep end-to-end suites that need containers or real browsers out of the regular unit-test run, and run them only in their own dedicated CI check.
rules.why: End-to-end suites against containerized identity providers and real browsers run in their own CI gate and never in the Definition of Done.
rules.check: Look for container- or browser-based end-to-end tests added to the default test run or the Definition-of-Done build instead of the dedicated end-to-end check.

rules.statement: In a backend-for-frontend, use a non-standard `refresh_token_expires_in` from the token response only to shorten the session's lifetime, never to extend it.
rules.why: OPs don't advertise a refresh token's absolute expiry in a standard way, so the BFF honors the value from any OP that sends it, but only as a cap on the session.
rules.check: Look for code that sets or extends a session expiry from `refresh_token_expires_in` without taking the minimum with the existing expiry.

rules.statement: In a backend-for-frontend, never send access or refresh tokens to browser code, including Blazor WebAssembly components: they call through the BFF using the session cookie.
rules.why: The BFF is the confidential client, and a WebAssembly client never holds a token.
rules.check: Look for endpoints, render-state or component parameters that serialize tokens to the browser or WebAssembly client.
